planting.note: Plant nursery-grown specimens in spring into very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in bright light with some direct sun; wear gloves when handling, since the melon-ribbed stem exudes an irritating milky latex sap if nicked or bruised.

directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun in a very well-drained, mineral-heavy succulent mix, watering only after the soil has dried out completely. The rounded, eight-ribbed stem resembles a small striped melon and slowly elongates into a squat cone shape with age, while old dried flower stalks persist as small woody, antler-like projections scattered over the surface, a signature identifying feature of this South African species. Growth is extremely slow, so resist the urge to overpot or overwater, both of which are the most common causes of stem rot in cultivation. Handle cut or damaged tissue with care and wash off any latex sap that contacts skin, since it is a caustic irritant typical of the genus.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Dragon Bone Tree (Mottled Spurge, Hatrack Cactus)

planting.note: Root calloused stem cuttings or plant container specimens in spring in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright light with some direct sun; wear gloves and eye protection, since the abundant milky latex sap is a strong skin and eye irritant.

directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering sparingly and only once the soil has dried out. This fast-growing tree-like Asian species produces tall, three- to four-angled candelabra stems marked with an attractive irregular white or pale-green mottling along the ridges, distinct from the crested, coral-like mutant form of the same species sold separately as 'Cristata'. Small black thorns line the ridges, and the plant branches readily from cuts or breaks to form a dense, upright thicket over time. Cut ends should be allowed to callus for several days before rooting, and any spilled latex sap should be rinsed from skin immediately, as it is a potent irritant and mildly toxic if ingested.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Red African Milk Tree (Rubra Cathedral Cactus)

planting.note: Root calloused stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, placed in bright light with several hours of direct sun to develop deep burgundy coloring; handle only with gloves, since the milky latex sap is a severe skin and eye irritant.

directions: Grow in bright light with several hours of direct sun daily, in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only after the soil has dried out completely. This selection of African milk tree carries the same upright, triangular, ridged stems as the green species but flushes a deep wine-red to burgundy across the new growth, an effect that intensifies with stronger light and fades toward green in shadier spots. Propagate from stem cuttings allowed to callus for several days before potting, since fresh-cut latex otherwise inhibits rooting and the sap is a potent skin and eye irritant that calls for gloves and eye protection whenever pruning. Repot every couple of years into fresh, fast-draining mix, and keep away from children and pets given the plant's toxicity if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; ammak euphorbia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, and all cut surfaces exude a caustic milky latex that demands gloves and eye protection.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, watering deeply but infrequently once roots establish. Native to the mountains of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, this columnar candelabra succulent forms a stout central trunk topped by tiers of ascending, four- to five-angled spiny branches, giving mature specimens a strongly architectural, tree-like silhouette prized in desert landscaping. A white-variegated sport is also widely grown in cultivation and is often even more common in the nursery trade than the plain green species, though it needs slightly more shade to avoid scorching. All parts contain a corrosive, milky latex sap that severely irritates skin and eyes and is toxic if ingested, so prune only with heavy gloves and eye protection and site well away from children, pets, and foot traffic.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Indian Spurge Tree (Milk Hedge, Hedge Euphorbia)

planting.note: Root calloused stem cuttings or plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to partial shade; wear gloves when pruning, since the freely flowing latex sap is a strong irritant traditionally used with caution in folk medicine.

directions: Grow in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, gritty soil, watering deeply but infrequently and allowing the soil to dry between waterings. Thick, spiny, angled stems bear fleshy, oleander-like leaves that are shed in dry conditions and regrown with rain, a trait that sets this South and Southeast Asian species apart from the leafless succulent Euphorbias more commonly grown as houseplants. Long cultivated as a living security fence and hedge throughout its native range, it is also the standard hardy rootstock onto which many colorful crested and variegated Euphorbia cultivars are grafted. Handle pruning cuts with gloves and eye protection, since the copious milky latex is a potent skin and eye irritant and is toxic if ingested.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Start from fresh seed or pot up self-sown seedlings in spring in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light; ripe seed capsules split open explosively and scatter seed, so this species readily self-sows around the base of established plants.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light or morning sun in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, watering moderately and letting the top inch of soil dry between waterings. A single slender, cane-like stem is topped by a whorled rosette of lance-shaped, dark green leaves boldly marked with prominent white or cream veins, giving this Madagascar species a striking, almost tropical-houseplant look distinct from the spinier desert Euphorbias. Small greenish flowers give way to three-lobed seed capsules that dry, pop open, and fling seed several feet, so established plants often produce volunteer seedlings nearby. As with other Euphorbias, all cut or broken tissue releases a milky latex sap that irritates skin and eyes, so handle pruning and repotting with gloves and keep away from children and pets.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container specimens in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun for the brightest spine color; wear thick gloves, since both the sharp spines and the irritating milky latex sap require careful handling.

directions: Grow in full sun in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out completely, since this South African species is extremely drought-tolerant once established. Slender, cylindrical, ribbed stems cluster from the base and are densely set with persistent, bright coral-red to pink spines that give the plant its common name and its best color in strong light. Older stems gradually turn woody and grayish at the base while continuing to produce fresh spiny growth above, and offsets can be removed and rooted to form new clumps. Handle with heavy gloves, since beyond the sharp spines the plant exudes a caustic milky latex when cut that irritates skin and eyes and is toxic if ingested.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container specimens in spring in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; the exceptionally long paired spines and caustic latex sap make heavy gloves and eye protection essential when handling.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, very well-drained soil, watering sparingly and allowing the soil to dry fully between waterings. Broad, zigzagging, three-angled stems are armed along each wavy margin with remarkably long, sharp, paired spines that curve outward like a pair of cow horns, a dramatic feature that has made this East and Southern African species a popular barrier or security planting in frost-free gardens. Branching stems build into a dense, tangled thicket over time, and older growth toward the base can become woody and less angular. Because both the formidable spines and the abundant milky latex sap pose real hazards, prune and repot only with heavy gloves and eye protection, and site away from paths, children, and pets.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
